title: BAR U3·W3 — Technical Reporting: Lessor Leases, R&D & Software Costs (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the harder accounting BAR owns

BAR's technical-reporting area takes selected topics deeper than the FAR core. This week covers the lessor side of leasing (FAR Unit 1 built the lessee side), the research and development rules that expense innovation, and the nuanced software-cost capitalization rules that split internal-use from for-sale software. These are the judgment-heavy areas — when to capitalize, when to expense — that a discipline-level CPA must apply, and where MBG's investment in a custom job-cost system gets its accounting.

Lessor lease classification

Under ASC 842, a lessor classifies each lease as sales-type, direct financing, or operating. A lease is a sales-type lease if it meets any of the same criteria that make a lessee's lease a finance lease — transfer of ownership, a reasonably certain purchase option, a lease term for the major part of the asset's life, the present value of payments equals substantially all of fair value, or a specialized asset with no alternative use. If none are met but the lessor still recovers its investment plus a return through payments and a third-party residual guarantee, it is direct financing; otherwise it is an operating lease.

Sales-type and direct-financing leases

In a sales-type lease, the lessor effectively sells the asset: at commencement it derecognizes the asset, records a net investment in the lease (the present value of payments plus any residual), and recognizes selling profit immediately (the difference between the fair value and carrying amount) — plus interest income over the term. A direct-financing lease defers any selling profit into the net investment and recognizes it as interest income over time. Both put a receivable, not the asset, on the lessor's books — the financing view of the arrangement.

Operating leases (lessor) and the symmetry

In an operating lease, the lessor keeps the asset on its books, continues to depreciate it, and recognizes lease income on a straight-line basis over the term. There is an important asymmetry to remember: lessor and lessee classifications are tested separately and need not match in label, though they use related criteria. For a contractor that both leases equipment to others and leases its own, understanding both sides prevents the common error of assuming the two parties mirror each other's accounting.

Research and development costs

Research and development (ASC 730) costs are expensed as incurred — both the research (planned search for new knowledge) and the development (translating findings into a plan or design) phases. The rationale is the high uncertainty that R&D will produce future benefit. The key exception: materials, equipment, or facilities with an alternative future use are capitalized and depreciated (the depreciation on R&D equipment is itself an R&D expense). Costs incurred for others under a contract are not the company's R&D expense — they are costs of providing a service.

Internal-use software

Software developed for the company's own use (ASC 350-40) follows a three-stage model. Costs in the preliminary project stage (conceptual evaluation, alternatives) are expensed. Costs in the application development stage (coding, configuration, testing) are capitalized. Costs in the post-implementation/operation stage (training, maintenance) are expensed. The capitalized asset is then amortized over its useful life. So MBG's spending to build a custom job-cost system is expensed during planning, capitalized during build, and expensed again once it goes live — the stage, not the type of cost, drives the treatment.

Software to be sold or marketed

Software developed to be sold, leased, or marketed (ASC 985-20) turns on technological feasibility. Costs incurred before technological feasibility (the detailed program design or a working model) are expensed as R&D. Costs incurred after technological feasibility, until the product is available for general release, are capitalized. Capitalized software costs are then amortized at the greater of the straight-line amount or the ratio of current revenue to total expected revenue. The technological-feasibility threshold is the dividing line the exam tests.

Putting the capitalization rules together

The unifying theme is when future benefit becomes probable enough to capitalize. Pure R&D is too uncertain — expense it. Internal-use software crosses the line at the application-development stage; for-sale software crosses it at technological feasibility. Misapplying these triggers either overstates assets (capitalizing too early) or understates them (expensing capitalizable costs), distorting both the balance sheet and the expense pattern. Recognizing which framework applies — and where its trigger falls — is the core skill this week builds.

Lease remeasurement and other lessor topics

Several refinements complete lessor accounting. A lessor remeasures the net investment when a lease is modified in a way that is not a separate contract, and tests the net investment (and any unguaranteed residual) for impairment using the credit-loss model. Initial direct costs are deferred and recognized over the lease term for direct-financing and operating leases, but expensed at commencement for a sales-type lease that recognizes selling profit. Sale-leaseback transactions require determining whether a real sale occurred under ASC 606 before applying lease accounting. These nuances show that the lessor model, like the lessee model, is built on the same control and revenue concepts running through GAAP.

Cloud computing and other intangibles

The software rules extend to modern arrangements. Costs to implement a cloud-computing (hosting) arrangement that is a service are capitalized using the same model as internal-use software (capitalize the application-development-stage implementation costs) and amortized over the term of the service contract. Start-up and organization costs, by contrast, are expensed as incurred, and most internally generated intangibles (brands and customer lists developed internally) are not capitalized at all. Knowing which costs attach to an asset and which are period expenses is the same capitalize-versus-expense judgment that governs R&D and software.

Disclosure and the leveraged lease

Lease accounting carries robust disclosure requirements: lessors disclose the components of the net investment, lease income by type, and a maturity analysis of lease receivables. A leveraged lease grandfathered under prior guidance continues its specialized accounting until it ends. The disclosures give users insight into the timing and risk of the lessor's lease cash flows — the same transparency objective that runs through every reporting standard in this unit.

CMA bridge

When MBG invests in equipment leasing or builds its own software, BAR decides the accounting the CMA program then reports. The lessor rules determine whether a leased asset becomes a receivable; the software rules determine how much of a system build sits on the balance sheet — both directly affecting the asset base and the margins the CFO analyzes.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify lessor leases: sales-type (finance criteria met → derecognize asset, net investment, immediate selling profit) vs direct financing (defer profit into interest income) vs operating (keep/depreciate asset, straight-line income).
  2. Expense R&D as incurred (ASC 730); capitalize only materials/equipment with alternative future use.
  3. Internal-use software (350-40): expense preliminary + post-implementation; capitalize application-development stage.
  4. For-sale software (985-20): expense before technological feasibility, capitalize after until release; amortize at the greater of straight-line or revenue ratio.

Recap: a lessor records a sales-type lease as a sale (derecognize the asset, book a net investment, recognize selling profit and interest), a direct-financing lease by deferring profit into interest income, and an operating lease by keeping and depreciating the asset with straight-line income; R&D is expensed as incurred except for assets with alternative future use; internal-use software capitalizes only the application-development stage; and for-sale software capitalizes costs after technological feasibility until release, amortized at the greater of straight-line or the revenue ratio.

flashcards.back: Sales-type (any finance-lease criterion met), direct financing (recovers investment + return via payments and third-party residual guarantee), or operating (neither).
Derecognize the asset; record net investment in the lease (PV of payments + residual); recognize selling profit immediately + interest income over the term.
Defer any selling profit into the net investment and recognize it as interest income over time. Receivable on the books, not the asset.
Keep and depreciate the asset; recognize lease income straight-line. Lessor and lessee classifications are tested separately and need not match.
Expense both research and development as incurred. Exception: materials/equipment/facilities with alternative future use are capitalized and depreciated.
Preliminary project stage: expense. Application development stage: capitalize. Post-implementation/operation: expense. Then amortize the capitalized cost.
Expense costs before technological feasibility (as R&D); capitalize after feasibility until available for release; amortize at the GREATER of straight-line or revenue ratio.
Capitalize when future benefit is probable enough: internal-use at the application-development stage; for-sale at technological feasibility; pure R&D never (too uncertain).

questions.q: In a sales-type lease, the lessor at commencement:
choices: Derecognizes the asset and recognizes selling profit
Keeps the asset and depreciates it
questions.explain: A sales-type lease is treated as a sale: derecognize the asset, record a net investment, and recognize selling profit plus interest income.

questions.q: A lessor's operating lease income is recognized:
questions.explain: In an operating lease the lessor keeps the asset and recognizes lease income on a straight-line basis.

questions.q: Research and development costs under ASC 730 are generally:
questions.explain: R&D is expensed as incurred; only materials/equipment with alternative future use are capitalized.

questions.q: For internal-use software, costs in the application development stage are:
questions.explain: ASC 350-40 capitalizes application-development-stage costs; preliminary and post-implementation costs are expensed.

questions.q: For software to be sold, capitalization begins when:
questions.explain: ASC 985-20 expenses costs until technological feasibility, then capitalizes until the product is available for release.

questions.q: Equipment purchased for an R&D project that has an alternative future use is:
questions.explain: Assets with alternative future use are capitalized; their depreciation is charged as R&D expense.

questions.q: Capitalized software-for-sale costs are amortized at:
choices: The greater of straight-line or the revenue ratio
questions.explain: Amortization is the greater of the straight-line amount or the current-to-total expected revenue ratio.
